summary.text: Paleographic interpretations identify 午 as a picture of a pestle, the implement also written 杵. A conventional account proposes that the graph was borrowed for the seventh earthly branch because the old tool-name and branch-word sounded alike; the tool’s ancient name and that sound match are unresolved. 午 is also used for midday, but its relation to the branch use is unclear.

formation.text: Pictographic: paleographic accounts interpret the whole early graph as a pestle, a rod thick at both ends and narrow in the middle. The accounts describe later graphic changes in bronze forms, Chu manuscripts, and seal script. These are source interpretations; the glyph images were not visually inspected.

components.text: The whole graph is interpreted as a pestle or wooden pounding stick, thick at both ends and narrow in the middle. This is a pictorial reading, not an internal split; the implement’s ancient name and pronunciation are unresolved.

history.text: Paleographic accounts describe an early pestle-shaped graph. In later bronze forms, the upper part is said to reflect graphic corruption of one thick end; in Chu manuscripts and seal script, the lower thick end became a horizontal stroke. These reported interpretations describe graphic change, not observations made here from glyph images.

Other analyses identify the pictured object as a horse whip or reins. One account disputes the whip interpretation, noting a separate bronze graph for a whip. The implement’s ancient name and pronunciation remain unresolved.

uncertainties.text: A cited bronze inscription uses 午 as an earthly-branch sign, but the account does not date the vessel and therefore does not establish the first attestation of that use.

The proposed borrowing for the branch word depends on a sound resemblance between that word and the implement’s ancient name. Since that name and pronunciation are not recovered, the proposed match cannot be verified.

午 is recorded for the midday period, including 11 a.m.–1 p.m., and for the sun at its daily highest point. The cited examples do not establish when these uses began or a precise path from the branch name to them.
The Shuowen explanation connects 午 with yin and yang opposing in the fifth month. This is a historical account, not independent confirmation of the graph’s origin or the chronology of its meanings.

Analyses also associate 午 with ‘crosswise’ or ‘oppose’ and debate its relation and sound history with related graphs. The evidence does not establish these senses as the origin of the branch use or as a path to the midday meanings.

senses.text: Paleographic accounts identify the early graph as a pestle or wooden stick for pounding rice, and describe 午 as the original graph for the implement word 杵. This is an interpretation of the pictured object; its ancient name and pronunciation are unresolved.
A cited bronze inscription uses 午 in 庚午 as the seventh earthly branch. The vessel is undated in the cited account, so this attestation does not establish the earliest occurrence.

limitations.text: The cited records do not securely date the first branch or midday use, or establish the precise semantic path from the branch name to midday.

No sound comparison between the ancient name of the pictured implement and the branch word is available. Historical readings reported for 午 concern the branch or other senses, not an independently established name for the depicted tool.
